HOW WE TALK ABOUT THE ROOM — Corner and Cure

Warm, never fussy. We let the food carry the sentence.

Words we use: burnt butter, the good bread, scrubbed oak, the pass, a glass of something, most nights until late. Warm but never orange. Generous. Somebody cooked it.

Words we do not use: artisanal, curated, elevated, drizzle, deconstructed, journey. Nothing that sounds like a chain and nothing that sounds like a tasting menu.

The room: forty covers and a counter on the west side. Sandwiches and bowls at lunch. Small plates and wine once the pendants come on at four. Regulars who come twice a week and know the staff.

Example line we would write ourselves: "Small plates and a glass of something, most nights until late."

One rule that is not a style note: Danny's dish copy is final. Do not reword it, do not shorten it, do not re-space it. The allergen line matters and it stays exactly as written.

HOW WE PRESENT — Cedarline and Vale
From the principal.

Cool, restrained, true. We sell architect-designed homes to buyers who read light as build quality and who are looking at three other agents' listings on the same afternoon. Our credibility is that the pictures are the house.

What I mean by cooked: any picture that has been pushed until it stops looking like the room. Skies dropped in, grass turned fluorescent, whites gone blue, blacks crushed to nothing, a window "view" that is obviously not the view. If a buyer can tell it was retouched, we have lost them. I would rather a window be named as not deliverable than faked.

Type and layout: quiet. Generous margins, one photograph doing the work, nothing that announces itself. Not warm and cosy, not developer gold-and-black.

One housekeeping thing for the window run: we went under contract on 51 Alder Court last week. The office manager has not pulled it off the active export yet, so it will still be in whatever you were sent. Leave it out of the window cards, please, it should not be advertised. That leaves the six existing plus Ridgeway.

THE THREE HOUSES, AND WHAT WE DO NOT WANT DONE TO THEM
From the owner. Verranza Coastal Retreats.

We let three houses above the cove at Punta Verranza:
- Casa Verranza, sleeps 6. The oldest, warm and simple, the one my grandfather bought.
- Casa Oliveto, sleeps 8. In the olive grove, a green terrace sail for the heat.
- Casa Scogliera, sleeps 10. On the rocks, the biggest, the best sea view. It sleeps ten, not nine, whatever the sheet says.

We sold the fourth house, Casa Fienile, last year. It is not ours to let any more and must not go to agents.

Seasons, the way we quote agents: we call them Spring, High Summer and Autumn. If the booking sheet has them as S1, S2 and S3, that is Spring, High Summer, Autumn in that order. Please put the words agents know on the cards, not the codes.

The do-not-want list, in my words: nothing cooked. No water a colour that water is not. No stone turned into a computer's idea of stone. No fake evening glow, no orange skin, no crushed blacks. Anders and I have both arrived somewhere the pictures had lied and we will not do that to a guest. A guest choosing between our own three houses should not be able to tell they were shot on different days. That is the whole job.

And the mark: the monogram the village smith cut for my grandfather is the only one there is. Give it back to us as something we can place anywhere, small on a card and reversed out of our deep blue, and still have it be ours.

KESTREL AND VANE - HALCYON QUARTER, NOTES FOR THE DESIGNER

What we sell is the evening. Blue hour. The water should look cold and the rooms should look warm. Brass, not gold. Nothing shiny.

Quiet and expensive. Our buyers are leaving houses they have owned for thirty years, they are not impressed by a starburst or a sunset, and they will count the windows when they visit the site. If a picture shows something the building will not have, that is the one thing we cannot survive.

Phase one is four apartment types: the Loom, the Spindle, the Ropewalk and the Warehouse. That is the set. (The Reel was pulled from phase one; if it is still in the sales export, it is not for sale yet and should not get a card.)

Kestrel Home Lending's wording on the payment cards is theirs. Every line of it, including the rate and the term and the small print, is regulated. Do not edit it, shorten it, re-space it or abbreviate it, and do not let any of it get clipped. If you cannot fit a line, tell us, do not trim it.

Type: a proper text serif with real hierarchy, prices set plainly inside the copy, generous margins, one photograph per canvas. No hex from us, no measurements, that is your craft. Just: quiet and expensive.

WHAT WE KNOW, AND WHAT WE DO NOT WANT TOUCHED
Typed by Ruth (Ada's daughter). Two pages, kept since the nineties.

The photographs, oldest first:
- 1912, Brattleboro. Ada as a baby. The oldest one, a studio card, in the black album.
- 1931, Brattleboro. Ada as a young woman, in the album too.
- The wedding of Ada and Walter. The catalogue says 1938 but the back of the print is written in Ada's own hand "June 1936", and Mother was always sure of it. Use 1936.
- 1948, the porch, Ada with me as a baby.
- 1955, Putney, Ada with the three of us (me, Frank and Carol) in front of the old house. NOTE: cousin Dale sent this same photograph round again a few years ago under his own name for it and with the year as 1956. It is the SAME picture. We only need it once.
- 1967, the garden. Gone very orange.
- 1971, at the stove. This is the one with the SCAR on Nan's left hand, from the stove years before. A reprint somebody paid for in the eighties took the scar out and I have never forgiven it. The scar STAYS. Do not remove it, do not tidy it, do not smooth it.
- 1969, Nan with baby Tom.
- 1974, Nan in the garden chair, near the end.

Things that are the photograph, not damage, and must stay: the scar; the grain; the paper texture and deckled edges; the little pencil retouching the old studio did on Nan's cheek in the 1931 card; anything actually in the picture.

Quiet, please. Like a museum, not a memory book. Tell us what you corrected and what you left, and why.

GABLE & GROVE — A PAGE FROM MICHAEL (owner). How we want to look, and what we do not.

The yard signs are printed in our deep green. The sign shop has it as Grove Green, #1E3A2F. Everything green on our stuff is that green, nothing brighter.

The mark. The fellow who drew it for us is gone, packed up his shop two years back, and never sent the file. What we have is the picture he emailed us once and a photo of it painted on my own truck door. That mark means the house peak and the trees, it is a maker's stamp, not a sale sign. It has to work from a shirt to a yard sign, and on a yard sign it sits on the green.

The money and the people. We run between forty-five and a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a project. Our people are fifty to sixty-five, they own old houses and they are not in a hurry. They are getting two or three bids and they buy on trust, not on the lowest number. We sell everything twice, once on the site and once out of a quote pack on somebody's kitchen table.

When I say I don't want it looking HGTV, I mean the afters cannot look like a supermarket flyer or a paint-can ad. No fake blue skies, no cranked-up green grass, no glow. Cool, calm, real stone, honest blacks, one photograph doing the work. The befores stay exactly as honest as they came off the phone, because the before is the whole proof. If a before looks improved, we are lying, and these people can smell it.

One thing on permissions. The CHAPIN ROAD homeowners were very good to us but they have asked us NOT to publish anything from their job — no photos in the quote pack, on the site, on the showroom board, anywhere. Everything else last season is cleared to show. Please leave Chapin Road out and just tell me you did.

— M.

NATIONAL VEHICLE MARKETPLACE — SELLER FIRST-IMAGE STANDARDS
(copied off their seller help page — this is what keeps bouncing our listings)

EVERY listing's FIRST image (the primary tile) must meet ALL of the following or the listing is rejected:

1. SUBJECT: the vehicle only, fully within the frame, all four corners of the vehicle visible, with clear space ("air") on every side. No part of the vehicle cropped off.

2. BACKGROUND: a plain, single, neutral background. Nothing else in the frame — no other vehicles, no people, no signage, no forecourt clutter. A pure white or a plain neutral studio background is accepted; a clean transparent cut-out composited onto a plain ground is accepted.

3. NO ADDED GRAPHICS OF ANY KIND on the primary image: no dealer logo, no manufacturer badge overlay, no watermark, no border or frame, no starburst, no price sticker, and NO text of any kind burned into the image.

4. DIMENSIONS: primary tile minimum 1600 x 1200 px, exact 4:3 aspect ratio, JPEG or PNG, sRGB, file under 8 MB. Images below 1600 x 1200 are rejected; the platform does NOT upscale for you.

5. The primary image is shown on the platform's own listing grid on a LIGHT GREY card (#ECECEC), so cut-out edges must read cleanly against that grey, not only against white.

COMMON REJECTION REASONS we have hit:
- "Primary image contains added text or graphics" (our old cards had the dealer roundel burned in)
- "Background not plain" (other cars visible in the lot)
- "Image below minimum dimensions"

Images AFTER the first (positions 2+) may carry our own branding and design freely.

OSTRA — how we talk about the room, and the courses spelled the way the kitchen spells them.

THE ROOM. Twenty-two seats around the pass, one seasonal tasting menu at a hundred and thirty-five dollars a head, four nights a week. Near black, spare, unhurried. One plate at a time. The photographs should feel like walking into the room, not like an advertisement. Quiet, dark, unhurried. Not a bistro and not a hotel restaurant.

FOR THE STUDIO'S DESIGNER. We need FINISHED photographs from you, not raw files. Your build is dark: near black ground, very little on the page, one plate at a time, mobile responsive. The plates have to read as one set scrolled one after another, and they also have to survive the delivery platforms, which put every picture on a WHITE card in a grid next to everybody else.

COURSE TITLES — spell them EXACTLY like this on every card (this is this season's menu):
  Course 1: Oyster, sea buckthorn, frozen cucumber
  Course 2: Georges Bank scallop, browned butter, chervil
  Course 3: Maine lobster, fennel, saffron bisque
  Course 4: Dry-aged duck, quince, elderberry
  Course 5: Sea-salt caramel, brown-butter ice cream

VARIANT SUBSTITUTIONS (keep the same spelling):
  Pescatarian: Course 4 becomes 'Georges Bank halibut, fennel, brown butter'
  Vegetarian:  Course 3 becomes 'Charred hispi cabbage, caper, brown butter'; Course 4 becomes 'Roasted celeriac, quince, hazelnut'

PAIRING FLIGHTS: 'Cellar', 'Reserve Cellar', 'Zero-Proof'. A guest with no flight gets no pairing block — do not leave a blank line where the flight would be.

A note on the words: it is 'browned butter' on the scallop and 'brown-butter' on the caramel. Yes, on purpose. Spell them as written.

ARGENT & FAITH — HOW WE TALK ABOUT THE WORK (Nora)

Cold light, warm hand. The silver should sit cool and true, the way it looks under the north window, not warmed up and not blued out.

Oxidised recesses stay dark. Do not lift them. The dark in a channel is the drawing.

Nothing bright, nothing bouncing. No hot speculars blown to paper white, no glare. The metal leads and the type recedes.

The negative space in a band or a piercing is the design. A filled centre or a closed piercing is not our work.

Plenty of air. The piece sits small and centred with room around it. Quiet.

If a stone is in it, the stone should read as its own colour, not go grey.

GIRDERMARK — HOW TO TELL THE FINISHES APART (sales)

Galvanised: the spangled dull one. Dull grey with the crystal pattern in it. Not shiny.

Zinc plate: the bright bluish one. Clean and bright with a slight blue tint. Do not let it go grey and do not let it go brassy.

Clear anodised: the flat grey one. A flat even grey with no blue and no spangle. Do not let it collapse into the powder coat.

Powder coat: the flat black one. Dead flat, even black, no shine.

A buyer specifies a finish off the picture. If plated steel looks brassy or anodised looks the same as powder coat, they stop trusting the numbers next to it. Keep the four clearly different from each other.

- Never orange, never crunchy, never that filtered look. If skin has gone orange or the blacks have gone crushed, it is wrong.
- Hold the black point open. We do not crush shadows.
- Keep colour honest. Greens of the garden stay green, whites stay white, skin stays warm but real.
- One look that holds across the whole day: the window-lit ceremony, the last hour of sun in the walled garden, and the reception under the venue's own lights should all read as one gallery, not three different edits.

Standing rule: if a frame will not take the house pass, pull it and tell us. We would rather you pull a frame and tell us than force it. Do not ship a forced frame at eighty percent.

# Palewell Health -- internal brand notes

There is no brand book. This is it.

## Colour, in words
- A DEEP SLATE, close to a blue-grey charcoal. This is our ground; the header sits on it.
- A WARM CHALK, an off-white with a little warmth in it, for pages and space.
- ONE muted SIGNAL colour, a soft sage green, used sparingly for a link or a small accent. Never more than one accent.
- A soft ink for body text, and a near-white paper white.

## Tone
Plain, warm, unhurried. We speak to a person, not a patient. No hype, no superlatives, no clinical jargon. Example line we would write: "Manage the everyday stuff with someone in your corner, from home."

## What we mean by calm
Real rooms, ordinary daylight, generous air, restrained type. Faces that are present, not beaming. Not a hospital (never cold, sterile, blue). Not a wellness brand (never glossy or cosmetic). Not concierge (never near-black and sparse). Calm, credible, human.

# Cordwain Overland -- brand sheet (how we brief the printer)

## Palette, in words
- BASALT: a near-black warm charcoal. Our workhorse ink.
- TRAIL SAND: a muted tan/oat. Good on dark garments.
- PINE SHADOW: a deep muted green.
- RUST RIDGE: a burnt orange accent, used sparingly.
- BONE: a warm off-white, our light garment colour and a light ink.

## Placement rules (we have always used these)
- Full back: centred, top of print 3 inches below the collar seam.
- Chest: left chest OR centred chest depending on the graphic.
- Badge: centred chest on hoodies.

## Maximum print widths
- Full back: 12 inches wide max.
- Centre chest: 10 inches wide max.
- Left chest: 4 inches wide max.
- Hoodie badge: 3.5 inches wide max.

## What we mean by a tight print
Two or three tight inks with a bit of texture. Honest registration. We would rather run fewer inks well than a muddy six-colour job. Never price the line out of its own customers -- the printer charges per screen.

PRODUCTS
  Hard enamel lapel pins and struck challenge coins. Six designs, two products each.

  Coin thickness: 3.0 mm struck.

  COLOUR CEILING: maximum 5 enamel colours per design, plus the metal line. Do not exceed.

  Simplify detail out rather than leaving it and hoping — a pin is not a coin.
  Pin plating: polished gold or black nickel.

  The raised-metal face must be LINE ONLY: closed line work in raised metal against a recessed field. NO filled interiors where struck metal should show through.
  Minimum raised line 0.20 mm at struck diameter.
  Coin plating options: struck gold, antique silver, antique bronze.

CREST COLOURWAYS
  Supply 2–3 crest colourways shown ON THE STRUCK METAL (not swatches on white) for the committee to choose the flagship.

HANDOFF
  One vector file per design per product, closed paths, colours within the ceiling, diameter stated in the file. Put edition size on the capsule insert, never on the die.

QUAYSIDE HAND PRESS — notes for the Wharfside twentieth-year run (from Del & Marina, two streets up)

How we print. Everything is pulled by hand on the flatbed. We run FOUR inks plus the colour of the paper. The paper is one of your colours, so leave it working, do not flood it. On the shirt we can only give you TWO inks, no paper showing through as a colour because the cloth is the ground.

Stock.
- Poster: 300gsm uncoated kraft-toned board, natural oatmeal (about #E4D6BC). This is the big one for the shed and shop windows. True printed size 500 x 700 mm, portrait.
- Handbill: same natural oatmeal stock at 170gsm, trimmed to A5, 148 x 210 mm portrait. Same design as the poster, not a new one.
- Shirt: natural undyed cotton, print area about 300 mm wide across the chest.

Inks we are mixing for you: harbour blue, rust red, hill ochre, deep ink. If you need a fifth you have to drop one, we cannot run five plus the paper.

Registration. Hand pulled, so give us corner crop marks on all four corners AND one centre cross target, common to every plate so we can line them up. Expect 1 to 1.5 mm of slop between plates, so trap anywhere two solids butt: overlap the lighter ink under the darker by about 1 pt. Tell us on the spec which plate traps under which.

Line and tone. Minimum positive line 1.5 pt (about 0.5 mm). Minimum reversed (paper knocked out of ink) 2 pt or it fills in. We can only hold a COARSE dot by eye, roughly 20 to 25 lines to the inch, no fine screens and no process rosettes. Pick the coarseness against the size the thing actually prints at, and tell us the number. A screen that looks right on the poster will plug on the handbill if you do not think about it.

Act cards. Same A6-ish card as last year, one act per card, run on the small press. Fourteen this year.

Deadline. Films / positives in our hands by 15 August. Anything after that and the twentieth year prints late.

From Iris — how we talk about the work (no hex, no measurements, do not turn this into ad copy)

Salt, iron, cold light. That is the whole feeling. Nothing shiny, nothing that shouts.

One ink doing the work, and plenty of air around it. The bottle should earn its place in a hand, not across a shop. If a version looks busy or clever it is wrong.

The wax is the colour of dried blood on the neck. The cap is cold grey. The crate is just the timber and one dark stamp. Keep it that quiet.

Write the supplier sheet like an instruction, not an advertisement. Say plainly what a version can and cannot do. And if something in our own list looks wrong to you, say so before you make it.

Four forwarded supplier messages (pasted by the founders)

--- 1. FROM: Aldous Wax & Seal Co. ---
We pour your neck seals from a single stamping die. We need the mark as ONE solid vector, black on transparent, no tints, no hairlines under 1mm, and nothing enclosed that has to stay open — our die floods any counter smaller than about 2mm. Last batch you sent a file with a fine rope outline and it filled solid on the seal. Send us the plate you actually want stamped.

--- 2. FROM: Kerr Stencil Cutting ---
Stencils are cut on a plotter. One colour, and every shape must be a closed island the blade can lift — no open strokes, no shading, no cross-hatch. If it has more than a couple of thin bridges it falls apart on the crate. We need the simplest one-ink version you have.

--- 3. FROM: Northgate Closures (caps) ---
The cap emboss is tooled from a single-depth relief, so give us one flat shape, high contrast, no gradient and no fine line. Roughly 14mm across on the cap top. If the hull goes to a black blob at that size tell us and we will simplify.

--- 4. FROM: Redgate Print (labels) ---
We still hold your 2025 label file and can re-run it. Reminder it is set two-up on the cutter (front and back on one sheet) so whatever you change has to keep both. We never had the back copy as separate fields, it came to us as one block, so if you are re-flowing it be careful. No bleed on that die.

From the founder — what the mark is meant to mean (read it, then tell me what you think)

I made the main mark in an image tool at 2 a.m. two years ago. The two arms locking together are supposed to be two schedules meshing without a gap — that is the whole product, things fitting that usually do not. I know it is soft. I still like the glow, it feels calm, halcyon, which is where the name comes from. Tell me honestly what happens to that glow if you rebuild it, I would rather know.

The two sub-product marks I made later, separately, and they have never quite felt like the main one. If they should change to belong, change them.

Our buyers are engineers. They read fuss as sloppiness. Sharp, plain, restrained — no gloss for its own sake. If something in our own list turns out to be a bad idea, tell us before you build it.

NUMBER HEIGHT: you have always run an 8 inch tall number and it reads well from the far side of the road, so keep it at 8 inches unless you tell us otherwise. Any club letters that sit on the number line should be capped to that same 8 inch height.

MINIMUM STROKE: our cutter cannot hold a line thinner than 3 mm (about 1/8 inch) at final pressed size. Anything thinner than that lifts at the edge in the first wash and peels by June. If any part of the lettering comes in under 3 mm at 8 inch height, put it in your note and we will thicken it, or you will lose it on the press.

We press at 305 F for 15 seconds, so the film has to be one clean single shape with no tiny islands or closed-up holes. Send us one flat cut colour and we are good to go.

— Providence Print & Press

THE MARCHFIELD EXCHANGE — SIGN PROGRAMME SITE SURVEY
Prepared by: Halloran Brass & Engraving Co. (fabricator)
Surveyed on site: front elevation and ground-floor lobby.

MACHINE / PROCESS
Rotary and V-groove engraving into solid brass, satin finish, wax-filled lines. We engrave from vector geometry, not from a picture: a filled shape with the pattern painted on it is no use on the machine.
MINIMUM ENGRAVED STROKE WIDTH WE CAN HOLD AT FINAL SIZE: 0.50 mm. Any line finer than 0.50 mm at the size it is actually engraved will not cut cleanly and will either drop out or fill. This is the hard limit for the whole programme.

1. ENTRANCE PLAQUE (replaces the existing plaque)
   Size: 450 x 300 mm, landscape.
   Substrate: 6 mm solid cast brass, satin finish, wax-filled engraving.
   Fixing: 4 x M8 countersunk brass bolts into the limestone, one near each corner. Keep all artwork at least 15 mm clear of each bolt centre.
   Crest engraved at 180 mm across at the head; THE MARCHFIELD EXCHANGE engraved beneath in capitals.

2. DIRECTORY BOARD (lobby, replaces the plastic board)
   Size: 600 x 900 mm, portrait.
   Substrate: engraved brass face on an oak backing panel, satin finish.
   Fixing: concealed cleat brackets, top edge 1600 mm above finished floor. 20 mm clear margin all round; nothing in the outer 20 mm.
   Crest engraved at 120 mm across at the head; the tenant lines beneath in suite order.

3. SUITE PLATES (one per suite)
   Size: 200 x 75 mm, landscape.
   Substrate: 3 mm solid brass, satin finish, wax-filled engraving.
   Fixing: 2 concealed studs plus adhesive, no visible fixings on the face. 12 mm clear margin all round.
   Layout: crest engraved at 32 mm across at the left; suite number and firm name engraved to the right.
   NOTE: at 32 mm the crest's finest interior lines are the tightest test of the 0.50 mm minimum on the whole job. Check them here first before anything is committed.

GENERAL
- All panels are satin brass, so proofs must be judged on brass, not on white.
- We will quote per panel from your schedule. Tell us up front any line you already know falls under 0.50 mm at its final size so we can flag it rather than cut it.

KANTYNA NOVA — APPROVED COPY (course titles are set, do not rewrite)

Tagline: One seating. One menu. One evening.
About: A single table set once a night. One tasting, one wine flight, cooked and served by the two of us. The room is dark and quiet by design, so the plate is the only thing lit.
Voice: first person plural, plain, understated. Never salesy.

THE TASTING — fourteen courses, in order (page one of the menu)
1. Oyster, brown butter, sea lettuce — Cold, from the first minute of the evening.
2. Smoked mussel, celeriac, dulse — Smoke, then the sea underneath it.
3. Cured fluke, buttermilk, green apple — Cured that morning, dressed at the pass.
4. Sea urchin, potato custard, brioche — Set warm, a shard of brioche to break it.
5. Roasted beetroot, aged goat, walnut — Roasted whole in the ash, cut to order.
6. Hand-cut tagliatelle, brown crab, chilli — Rolled that afternoon, crab picked by hand.
7. Seared scallop, cauliflower, brown butter — One scallop, seared hard, brown butter to finish.
8. Halibut, leek, mussel cream — Poached soft, the cream built from the shells.
9. Duck, salsify, blackberry — Aged on the bone, blackberry from the reduction.
10. Dry-aged beef, bone marrow, burnt onion — Forty days, marrow and onion beside it.
11. Aged comté, honeycomb — Kept until it is ready, honey from up the coast.
12. Brown butter tart, sea salt — The pastry we make every day.
13. Chocolate, olive oil, malt — Dark, oil poured at the table, malt for the crunch.
14. Petit fours — Whatever we baked that morning. [NOTE: this course has never been photographed]

HOURS (for the reservations page)
Wednesday to Sunday. One seating a night. Doors at 6:30, seated at 7:00. Closed Monday and Tuesday.
The private dining side seats a smaller room on request.

RESERVATION WORDING (approved)
"One seating a night, and the room is small. Book the evening and let it happen — we will hold the table from 6:30. If your plans change, tell us as early as you can; there is no third of us to fill an empty seat."

THE DECK — how the price is built up (final slide, plain, price never a feature)
"The tasting is one hundred and eighty five dollars a guest. The wine pairing is another ninety five. That is the evening: fourteen courses, one flight, cooked and served by the two of us. There is no cover, no service charge added at the table, and nothing else to buy. Eighteen covers a night is the whole business, so the price is what it takes to set this table once and set it well."

CORNER & CURE — how we run the front of house (for whoever we hire next)

WHO WE ARE
A corner deli in Brooklyn. My father opened it, I run it now. Sandwiches, bowls, a cold case, a coffee machine. Twelve to sixteen dollars. People who work nearby and come in three times a week. We are warm, loud and unfussy. We are not fancy and we do not want to look it, but we are not cheap either and cheap is what this stuff usually looks like.

HOW WE TALK
Plainspoken, neighbourhood, a little brash, generous. The food does the talking. A line we would write: "Pulled together, piled high, see you at the counter." A line we would never write: anything that sounds like a chain, anything curated or elevated or artisanal.

HOURS
Mon-Fri 7am - 7pm. Sat 8am - 6pm. Sun 8am - 3pm. Coffee from open. Hot sandwiches all day. Cold case all day.

THE LOYALTY THING (goes on the register card)
Stamp card. Buy nine sandwiches or bowls, the tenth is on us. One stamp per visit. Ask at the register. No app, no points, no email.

THE WALL BOARD — sections, in this order
1. TODAY (the daily specials — these change EVERY DAY, so the board has to let us swap one tile without redoing the whole board)
2. SANDWICHES & HEROS
3. BOWLS & SALADS
4. FROM THE CASE
5. COFFEE & COLD DRINKS

A NOTE ON THE SPECIALS
The TODAY section changes daily. Whatever we build has to be something I can open myself and swap one special in and out in a minute, without touching anything else on the board. If a special needs a photo it comes off the counter shots.

A NOTE ON THE NAME
The sign over the slicer is the sign. It is our father's. Do not redraw it into a font. Whatever the window and the tags use, it has to still read as that sign, knife and all.

TAGLINE
One object at a time.

THE HOUSE
Maison Valcere is a four-person high-jewellery house, founded in 2014 in a room above a bookshop in Montreal. Twenty-two references sit in the current book, most cut and set by hand on one bench and shown by appointment. We work to order, for marriages and milestones, for clients who return once a decade rather than once a season.

PROVENANCE (fixed - do not reword)
Every Valcere piece is cut and set by hand on a single bench in Montreal. Stones are chosen one at a time and matched by eye. Metal is worked to the hand it is made for. A piece leaves the bench once, and it is meant to be kept.

APPOINTMENT
The autumn book is shown by appointment above the shop. Allow an hour. We bring out the pieces you ask for and the pieces beside them. Nothing sits on a floor; everything is made to your hand. Prices run nine hundred to six thousand five hundred dollars and are shown discreetly or on request.

FOR STOCKISTS
Maison Valcere is carried by a short list of stockists. Pieces ship on the house's own dark presentation band, so each piece must sit clean with no plate behind it. Metal, assay, stone and carat are stated on the card that travels with each piece; the assay wording is regulated and is not to be altered. Reorder by reference.

A NOTE ON THE MARK
The wordmark is the house. It is purely typographic - no symbol, no icon. Set in the house's high-contrast neoclassical caps with its grave accent and generous letterspacing, in House Black on Bench Ivory, or reversed in Signature White on House Black. It must still read as our wordmark at the size it sits on a boutique tile and reversed on our black, hairline serifs and accent intact.

NORDHEIM ATELIER - FW26 PRESS NOTES (approved copy; the two essay passages are the ones press will run)

SEASON NOTE
Twelve looks in undyed Gotland wool, Merino shearling and cotton gabardine. Cut on the straight, fulled at one mill in West Yorkshire, made by hand in Copenhagen. Cloth first.

ESSAY ONE - ON THE CLOTH
We started with the fleece and worked back. Undyed Gotland wool holds a grey no dye can give you, so we left it. The shearling is vegetable-tanned in Tuscany and turned so the skin reads as much as the wool. The gabardine is woven tight enough to hold an edge and cut so it falls straight. Nothing here is finished to hide the making; the seam is the seam and the button is horn. A coat should tell you how it was built when you pick it up.

ESSAY TWO - ON THE RANGE
This is one collection, not twelve pictures. We shot it over two days and lost the light on the second, and the work since has been to make the twelve read as one hand. The argument is restraint: held space, a hard black point, the cloth carrying the page. We would rather show you the shoulder of a coat than a styled room. If the range reads as one thing, the season has done its work.

PRESS RELEASE LINES
- Nordheim Atelier presents FW26: twelve looks, Copenhagen-made, in undyed wool, shearling and gabardine.
- Undyed Gotland wool, cut on the straight, made in Copenhagen.
- Available to press and to a wholesale list of roughly thirty independent stores. Delivery from August.

STOCKIST BOILERPLATE

ALDERWOOD SCHOLARS FUND -- TWENTIETH WINTER APPEAL (approved copy, do not edit)
The honour roll below cannot lose a single name.

=== APPEAL LANGUAGE ===
For twenty years, Alderwood Scholars Fund has run after-school learning centres in greater Providence and a small scholarship fund. This winter marks our twentieth year. Last year, ninety students finished the programme, and this appeal is where roughly half of our giving comes from.
We show our numbers plainly and we name where every dollar went, because our donors trust that the money reaches the students rather than the overhead. This year we opened our fifth centre, Cranston Fields, last September, so its first figures cover the months since it opened rather than a full year. Everything else covers the full programme year.
Twenty years is a milestone about the students, not about us. Thank you for being part of it.

=== THE ASK (for the donor deck's closing) ===
Our average gift is $45, and it matters. Our major asks this winter run from $5,000 to $50,000.
Closing line (major-donor meeting): "Will you consider a leadership gift of $50,000 to carry all five centres through the twentieth year?"
Closing line (general): "A gift of $5,000 funds a full year of tutoring for a centre's reading group. Will you join us?"

=== THREE CENTRE STORIES ===
WATERMAN ROW. When Priya took over the reading group at Waterman Row, eleven of her thirty-four students were reading below grade level. By spring, most had gained more than a full grade. "They stopped hiding the book under the table," she says. "They started asking to read out loud."

OLNEYVILLE GREEN. Olneyville Green runs the math group, and this year twenty-five of twenty-nine students finished. Danielle keeps a jar of worn-out pencils on her desk. "Every pencil in there is somebody's homework," she says. "That jar is the programme."

PAWTUCKET MILLS. Pawtucket Mills holds a family reading night in the old mill room under the painted tree. Parents read beside their children. "We didn't build it for the parents," Rosa says, "but they're the ones who cried."

MARISOL COVE - copy for the page and the brochure (approved, use as written)

Tagline: The quiet side of the coast.

WHAT IS HERE
- Fourteen rooms on the bluff, most looking out over the cove.
- A path from the terrace down to a small private beach.
- The dining room, for breakfast and for dinner.
- Wood stoves in the suites, and firewood laid on the cold evenings.
- No pool and no spa. The point of the place is the water, the light and being left alone.
- Parking, slow mornings, and two rooms that take dogs by arrangement.

THE DINING ROOM
Breakfast is for guests. Dinner is open to anyone by reservation, a short menu that moves with what the boats bring in. Book the dining room when you book the room; the tables go first on the weekends.

CANCELLATION
Cancel seven days ahead and we refund in full. Inside seven days we hold one night. We are a small house, and a late cancellation is a room we cannot fill.

THE SEASON
Autumn and winter are our quiet months and they are the best ones. The crowds are gone, the dining room is easy to get into, and an hour before sunset the light comes off the water and the whole cove goes gold. That is when to walk down. Bring a coat for after dark.

LUMEN QUARTERLY - AUTUMN ISSUE - FEATURE COPY (FINAL. Approved by the editor. Do not cut, do not paraphrase.)

[Note to the designer, not for print: this feature runs about a fifth longer than the Spring feature. It is final. All fourteen captions carry a credit line. Everything below is to be set as-is.]

HEADLINE: What the Wood Remembers

STANDFIRST: For forty years Emory Vaughn has built the same small boat the same way, in the same shed above Sennet Cove. On one long afternoon in October we watched him begin another - and learned that almost nothing about it is quick, and almost nothing about it is decided in advance. [SET OVER THE OPENING PHOTOGRAPH, on a tint of the picture, so the photograph still reads behind the words.]

BYLINE: Words by Nora Ellison. Photographs by Perrin Doyle.

BODY:

Emory Vaughn keeps the same length of chalk in the same coat pocket he has kept it in for longer than most of the boats on this reach have been afloat. He is seventy-one. The shed sits a hundred yards above Sennet Cove on a slope that has never been level, propped at its downhill corner on a granite block his father set there, and from the wide door you can see the whole working water of the cove: two lobster boats on their moorings, a skiff hauled out and turned turtle, and the grey line on the mud where the tide was an hour ago and is not now.

"People think the hard part is the shape," he says, before he has picked up a single tool. "The shape is the easy part. The shape is decided. The hard part is the wood, because the wood has not agreed to it yet."

He builds peapods - double-ended rowing and sailing boats, thirteen and fifteen feet, the kind of small workboat that was rowed out to tend traps along this coast a century ago and is now bought, mostly, by people who love the look of them and the quiet of them and the fact that they were made by a pair of hands and not pressed out of a mould in a shed on the other side of the world. He has built, by his own uncertain count, "somewhere past three hundred." He does not keep a list. "If I kept a list I would start comparing them," he says, "and they do not compare. Each one is the only one while I am on it."

The shape itself lives on the wall of the shed, and it is older than he is. It is a half-model - one side of a hull carved from laminated pine, glued up in stripes of light and dark so that when he wants to know a dimension he can lift the offsets straight off it. His father carved it, and his father's shape it remains, refined over the decades by nothing more violent than a spokeshave taken to it on the two or three winters when a boat came out and something about her did not sit right in the water. "You do not redesign her," he says of it. "You listen to the ones that swim funny and you take a whisper off the model, and in ten years you have a boat nobody would change." When there is a decision to make he lofts the lines out full size in chalk on a painted patch of the floor, kneeling, sweeping a long limber batten into a curve and pinning it and standing to look, and the loft is where the boat first exists at the size a person will actually sit in.

He has built the same hull the same way for forty years, and he still stops to look at the grain before the first cut. That is the thing you notice first, watching him: how much of the work is looking. He picks up a cedar board from the rack along the back wall, carries it to the door where the light is, and turns it, and turns it again, and holds it up so the low sun rakes across the surface and throws the grain into relief. He is reading it the way you would read a face. "This one wants to be a garboard," he says at last, of the plank that runs first and lowest against the keel, the one that takes the hardest twist. "You can see it wants to go round. You do not fight a board that wants to go round."

The backbone comes first - the keel, the stem, the sternpost - cut from oak, heavier and darker than the cedar that will skin it. He sets it up on the trestles in the middle of the floor and stands back from it, and for a while he does nothing at all but look, walking around it, crouching to sight along its length with one eye shut. "Fair," he says, which is the word that runs through everything he does. A line is fair when there is no place your eye catches on it, no flat, no bump, nothing that argues. You cannot measure fair. You can only see it, and he has spent fifty years teaching his eye to see it, and he does not entirely trust anyone else's.

Before any of it, though, come the tools, and he sharpens them the way other men say grace. The first half-hour of the day is a stone and a strop and not one board touched, and he will stop in the middle of the afternoon and go back to the stone if a shaving comes off ragged. "A dull tool does not cut cedar, it tears it," he says, "and a torn surface never takes finish right, and you will see it for the life of the boat." His plane irons are ground to a camber only he can read; his chisels are his father's, the boxwood handles worn to the shape of a hand that is not quite the shape of his own. He has bought exactly two new tools in thirty years. Everything else he keeps alive.

The planking is where the boat becomes a boat. Each plank is spiled - shaped so that its edge lands sweetly against the one below it - and then it has to be persuaded round the curve of the hull, which is where the steam box comes in. He fires it up on an old propane ring in the corner, and when the box is roaring he feeds a plank in and waits, and while he waits he does not fill the time. He stands. "Ten minutes to the inch," he says, of the timber's thickness, and he times it by feel more than by clock. When it comes out it comes out fast and hot and pliable and there is a short, urgent window in which two people bend it home and clamp it before it sets, and for those few minutes the quiet shed is all motion and short words, and then it is over and the plank is on and cooling into its new shape and he is looking at it again.

"A boat is not a drawing," he says, wiping his hands. "A drawing holds still. Water does not. So the boat cannot hold still either. It has to give a little everywhere, and to give the same everywhere, or it will find the one place you were mean with it and it will work there until it lets the water in."

The fastenings are copper - rivets and roves, set by hand, one person holding an iron on the head while the other peens the rove down over the shank with a light hammer, tap tap tap, a sound that carries out the open door and across the cove. He counts them in his head. A fifteen-foot boat takes upward of a thousand. He has driven, he supposes, some hundreds of thousands in his life, and he still lines each one up as if it were the first, because a rivet set crooked is a rivet that will weep. "Nobody sees the ones you get right," he says. "They only ever see the one you got wrong."

A boat like this takes him the best part of four months and he asks for it what a good used car costs, and by any honest reckoning of the hours that is far less than nothing. There is a wait - a little over a year now - and he keeps it in a school notebook by the door, one name to a page, and he telephones people himself when their turn comes because he does not use the computer his niece set up for him. The people who wait are not, mostly, people who need a boat. "They could buy a plastic one on a Tuesday and be rowing it on a Wednesday," he says, without scorn. "They are not waiting for a boat. They are waiting for this boat. I do not fully understand it and I am not going to argue them out of it." He is aware, in a way that plainly costs him something to say, that the thing he makes has quietly become a luxury, when it began its life as the cheapest way a lobsterman could get out to his traps. "That is the world's doing, not mine," he says. "I just kept making the same boat until the world changed around it."

He learned from his father, in this shed, and his father learned from a man in a shed two coves east who is long dead and whose name Emory still says with care. There is a line running back through those sheds that he is aware of holding, and it troubles him, quietly, that he can see the end of it from where he stands. He has had apprentices. Two stayed a season and left for money, which he does not begrudge them - "there is no money in this, there was never any money in this" - and one stayed three years and was good, genuinely good, and then moved inland to raise a family, which he begrudges nobody either. "You cannot ask a young person to be poor and patient at the same time," he says. "That is two hard things."

But he is not sentimental about it, or he does not let himself be for long. When you ask him whether it matters that the skill might not outlast him, he looks at the boat on the trestles for a while before he answers. "It matters to me," he says. "Whether it matters is not really my department. My department is this one. If I get this one right, that is the whole of what I can do about it."

You do not force cedar. You ask it, and then you wait to hear what it says back. He says something close to that late in the afternoon, when the sun has come round to the door and the shavings on the floor are lit up gold and the day's work is nearly done, and he is not performing it, he is just describing how the work goes, and it is the truest thing anyone could tell you about him. There is no hurry in the shed and there never has been. The boat will be finished when it is fair and fastened and not before, and it will go into the water in the spring, and someone will row it out onto a cove somewhere, and it will give a little everywhere, the same everywhere, and it will not let the water in.

He walks us to the door at the end. The tide has turned and is coming back up the mud. He looks at it the way he looks at everything, without hurry, reading it. "Same water," he says. "Every day. It does not get bored of it and neither do I." Then he goes back in to sweep the floor, because you always sweep the floor, because a clean floor is a sign that the day was done properly, and he has done every day properly for forty years, and he intends to do this one properly too.

[END OF BODY]

ALDERVALE MUTUAL - Compliance desk note for the producer kit
From: Eleanor Prewitt, Compliance Officer

What we will and will not sign, plainly.

WHAT COUNTS AS AN ADVERTISEMENT. Anything that reads as a sales pitch rather than a plain statement of fact. No superlatives, no urgency, no exclamation, no burst or starburst callouts, no implied guarantee of a return or of approval, no comparison that flatters us against a competitor. If a reasonable buyer at a kitchen table would feel sold to rather than informed, it does not go out. We are a ninety-one year old mutual; we look like one.

PRODUCERS ON PUBLISHED MATERIAL. Only a currently appointed, active producer may appear on a counter card or in any client-facing piece. If a producer's appointment has ended - resigned, terminated, lapsed - that producer must be removed before anything prints, regardless of what the licensing export still shows. The export lags; you check the status.

DISCLOSURES. The disclosure on a card or a client piece must appear exactly as written in the roster, word for word, and in full. A disclosure that is cut off, shortened, or stops before the sentence ends is a compliance failure and a regulatory exposure, not a design choice, even if the card looks fine otherwise. Producers licensed in more than one state carry that state's required language in full; it is longer, and it does not get trimmed to fit.

PHOTOGRAPHS. We may use a photograph of an appointed producer. We may NOT use a photograph of a policyholder, a client, or a real family, and we own none. If a piece needs an opening image that is not one of our own people, it must be a clearly licensed stock or illustrative image and it must be honest about being that.

RATES AND PLANS. When we show what a premium buys, the figures must be true to the pricing desk's table. Our three plans are not quoted the same way and must not be presented as one comparable set of numbers without a clear, plainly worded qualification that a family can read and understand. Do not put three differently based figures on one axis as though they were the same thing.

VOICE. Sober, plain, reassuring. A whole life policy is a promise that holds its value; say it like that. Nothing that sounds like a wealth manager and nothing that sounds like a mailer.

ANVIL AND OAK - how the programming works and what the levels mean (from Mara and Deacon)

WHO RUNS IT
Two of us. Mara Voss and Deacon Hale. We ran a barbell club out of a shared space for six years before this and about half our people are coming with us. We coach, we don't sell memberships you don't use.

HOW THE PROGRAMMING WORKS
Everybody is on one system. You warm up the same movements every week - squat, press, pull, carry - and the load moves in a planned way, not by feel. New people run a simple linear progression until the easy jumps stop, then we move them onto four-week blocks that alternate volume and intensity. We write the program; you show up and do the work and add weight. That is the whole pitch. Show up, do the work, add weight. We handle the programming so you can focus on the bar.

WHAT THE LEVELS MEAN (this is the Level column on the roster)
- FOUNDATIONS: learning the lifts, empty bar to first real loads, coached closely. No meet pressure.
- STRENGTH: the main room. Running blocks, chasing lifetime numbers, training three to four days.
- COMPETITION: peaking for a platform, training around meets, attempts and openers planned with a coach.

A FEW LINES ON THE ROSTER
This is the opening group, the ones following us over plus a few new Foundations people. Rosa, Theo, Nadia and Sam have been with us the whole six years. Priya, Bex and Fiona are new this winter and moving fast. Dot came back to lifting at fifty and out-trains people half her age.

ONE THING ON CONSENT (important, do not miss this)
Reggie Tran asked us, after we pulled the roster export, to keep him OFF the cards and off the social posts for now. He is still training and still on the roster spreadsheet, we just never took him out of the export. Do NOT make a card for Reggie and do NOT put his portrait in the spotlight set. Everyone else is fine to feature. If the card count comes out one short of the roster, that is why.

Apexguard Surface Systems - direction for the rollout

Premium, modern, performance automotive. Minimalist and confident. Not flashy, not factory catalog, not tuner.

No mascots. No vintage badges. No heavy gradients. No starbursts, no percentage flashes, no chrome bevels, no exclamation points. We state numbers and let them carry.

A full install runs eighteen hundred to six thousand dollars on a car worth sixty thousand, so it has to look like that. A dealer principal has to believe the ten year warranty printed beside the film, and a two hundred dollar tint-shop flyer kills that. Equally, do not push it into moody enthusiast car-culture; we are a supplier a dealer group puts on its reconditioning line, not an Instagram page.

The master mark and the three tier marks (Guard, Guard Pro, Guard Elite) have to read as one family. A dealer looks at all four and sees one supplier, not three products.

One restrained accent against a deep neutral. Confident spacing. Performance stated as a plain table, not a burst. Photography clean and even, not dramatic.

Kilnmore - what we keep losing when someone else designs for us

Clean lines, balanced colour, plenty of negative space, nothing fussy. Calm, full frame, one piece given room. Space is the argument.

The glaze is the point. Oatmeal has to stay oatmeal, ash has to stay ash, cobalt slip has to stay cobalt, bare clay has to stay warm. That is what a buyer chooses and what a stockist orders against, and it is what gets returned when it is wrong. Do not neutralise the four glazes into each other and do not push any of them toward a colour it is not.

One warm, legible type system. A quiet humanist serif for the mark, headings and range names; a clean sans for the specification tables so a stockist reads them without effort. Warmth without decoration. Nothing script, nothing ornamented.

We are considered studio ceramics. Not impulse marketplace: no tiled grid of nine pieces, no price flashes, no countdown, no exclamation colours. Not gallery austerity either: the pieces are made to be used, and a stockist has to be able to read the dimensions to order from them.

Plain and warm, the studio talking about its own work. Made to be used, made in small batches. No sale language, no urgency, no exclamation points.

Tell us if anything in our data looks wrong before it prints.

For my grandfather, Walter Fernwood
Read by Claire Ellis

[Emphasis is marked with *asterisks*. Please keep it as real emphasis in the book, not as plain text.]

My grandfather did not like a fuss, so I will try not to make one.

He was born in this town and he died in it, ninety-four years between, and he thought that was *plenty*. He was the son of a man who spent eleven seasons on the road with a travelling magic company, carrying cabinets in and out of theatres, and Walter used to say his father came home with *one trick* and it was knowing how to disappear when the dishes needed doing.

What I want to say is that he was *steady*. He mended things. He kept his tools clean. When my grandmother was ill he sat with her every afternoon and read to her, and he did not tell anyone he was doing it. That was the whole of him: he did the thing and he did not need it *seen*.

He loved that summer in 1968 more than almost anything, the lake, the children small, the light going pink over the water. Some of those pictures have not aged well. He would have said *neither have I*, and meant it kindly.

We are not going to brighten him up today. He would have hated that. We are going to keep him as he was, which was *enough*.

Thank you for coming. He would have said you did not have to. He would have been glad you did.

HARBORLINE REALTY -- a note from Dana on how we want to look (for the designer)

WHO WE ARE
Eight of us, one office on the harbour, since 2009. I run it. We list the whole mid coast book -- a three hundred and twenty thousand dollar corner-lot starter one week and a four and a half million place out on the point the next -- and both matter to us the same. We are grounded, coastal, understated. We describe the house, not ourselves, and we never oversell.

THE TWO OTHER SIGNS IN TOWN
One is a national franchise storefront: loud, red, everything shouting, the same template whether it is a cottage or a compound. The other is a discount flat-fee outfit that makes every listing look like a classified ad. We do not want to be either. When I say a sheet looks cheap I mean this: too much on the page, the price screaming, a photo that fights the type, blacks gone grey, a logo that is nearly ours but not.

THE TWO REGISTERS (this is the whole job)
The point estate at four and a half million sells to people over fifty with cash who read restraint as proof we can be trusted with the sale: one photograph, deep margins, quiet type, the price set small and sure. The corner-lot starter at three-twenty sells to first-timers under thirty-five who need the price, the bed count and the open-house time to reach them from across a room: brighter, denser, price forward. Style the whole book like the estate and the starters look empty and evasive; style it like the starter and the estate looks like volume work in front of a vendor paying a six-figure commission. Make the difference read -- but both still have to be obviously us.

THE MARK
The rope ring around a lighthouse with the H and the R is our mark. It is painted on the office window and that glass is the only place it still exists; the artwork was lost years ago. Whatever goes on the posts has to be that mark, recovered, knuckle for knuckle. Not something close to it, not redrawn into a font.

THE OPEN HOUSE POSTS
Prices move on Thursdays. Whatever you hand us for the open houses I have to be able to open and change a price in myself, in a minute, without paying anyone twice.

THE ROSTER
We should be carrying eleven active this week. The Sea Meadow cottage on Beauchamp went under agreement Thursday -- it should be off the run, but Monday's export may still have it in. If anything else looks off, ask me: two sheets went out last month with January's prices and I am not doing that again.

-- Dana Marlow

CEDARLINE INSTITUTE - autumn cohort, note from the Registrar's office (Helen Abbott)

For whoever is setting the credentials this year. Read this before you touch the export.

THE TWO PROGRAMMES
We run one subject, Professional Practice, at two very different registers, and they must never come off the press looking like the same document.
- The Community Evening Programme. A hundred and eighty dollars, one evening a week, mostly younger working adults. The credential is a Certificate of Completion. It is a warm, plain, honest thing and it goes on a kitchen wall. In the export these carry a programme code beginning CPE.
- The Executive Programme. Nine thousand dollars, bought by the candidate's employer, and the diploma ends up framed in an office where that person's own clients read it. It is a Diploma, heavier and more formal, and it is the one the sponsoring firms judge us by. In the export these carry a programme code beginning CXP.
There is no separate column that tells you which is which. The code is the only place it lives, so split the cohort off the code and nothing else.

WHO SIGNS WHAT
- Community certificate: two signatures - Helen Abbott, Registrar, and Callum Reyes, Community Programme Lead.
- Executive diploma: two signatures - Dr Miriam Voss, Director of Executive Education, and Helen Abbott, Registrar.
The signature lines are already on both old press files. Do not move them.

HONOURS
The executive diploma carries an honours line: With Distinction, With Merit, or Pass, and the grade is in the export for those candidates. Set it exactly as recorded.

NAMES
Every name is set the way that candidate spells it, accents and all. We have had complaints from graduates whose names were flattened. If a name looks as though an accent has been dropped or spelled around, ask me before you print it - do not guess.

THE SPONSORS
Two autumn cohorts ago a sponsoring firm told us the executive diploma looked like something printed off a website. That is the single thing we cannot repeat. If the executive credential reads like the evening certificate in a frame, we will hear about it within the week.

THE SEAL
The seal is ours - it is the Institute's own device, the cedar and the founding year, 1978. It is not to be reinvented or redrawn from imagination. Whatever seal ends up on these credentials has to be our seal, the same one pressed into the certificate on the wall of the hall.

CORRECTIONS
Names get corrected right up to the morning of the ceremony. Whatever the programme and the card are built in, I have to be able to open them and fix a spelling myself an hour before we start.

Learning that holds up. - H.A.

MARLOW GLAZES — a note from the studio, in plain words (no recipes here)

There are three glazes in the Marlow range this season and they are the whole point of it, so a word on each so you know what you are looking at.

OATMEAL is the reactive one. It breaks pale, almost bone, over any edge or throwing ridge where it runs thin, and it pools a soft warm brown down in the rings at the bottom of a bowl where it gathers. No two pieces pool exactly alike. It should read warm and matte-soft, not glossy, and the pale broken rim is part of it — do not lose it.

CELADON is the gloss one. Glassy, green-grey, a touch bluer where it lies thick. It is the one that shows everything: every highlight, every reflection of the light, and the bright line that runs along a rim is the glaze doing exactly what it should. It has to stay green-grey and must not be pushed blue, and the piece must keep its rim.

SLATE is the matte one. A dead flat dark grey-green that drinks the light and gives almost nothing back. No sheen at all. It photographs like a shadow if you are not careful, so it needs its own handling, and it must stay matte — the moment it looks wet or sheened it stops being slate.

They have to tell themselves apart on the page. A buyer orders by the glaze and receives a carton, so if the picture cannot separate an oatmeal from a slate we are the ones who hear about it. — G.

LANTERNWOOD FOLK FEST - committee note to the designer (everything else you need from us)

TICKETS
Sixty-five pounds a day. Two thousand capacity, two stages, fourteen acts across the weekend. Weekend and day tickets both. Under sixteens free with a paying adult.

THE TWO STAGES (please use these exact names on every page and both boards)
- The Barn Stage (the big one, in the old threshing barn)
- The Orchard Stage (the smaller one, out in the orchard by the cider tent)

THE HEADLINERS (this one matters)
Saturday is closed by The Hollow Pines on The Barn Stage.
Sunday is closed by Marla Vance & the Tallgrass on The Barn Stage.
Those two are the reason a lot of people bought a ticket. Whatever running order you settle on, they have to READ as the headliners, closing their own day, not buried in the middle of a list because that is where our spreadsheet happened to put them. Please do not sequence them as though they are just two more acts.

RUNNING ORDER
The line-up sheet is in the order we booked people, which is NOT the order the weekend runs in. The programme has to run in the order the acts actually go on, so someone standing in the field can find who is on next. Two stages running at the same time makes that a judgement rather than a plain sort, so tell us in the note how you decided.

THE LICENCE LINE (must appear in the programme, word for word)
'Lanternwood Folk Fest is run under a Temporary Event Notice granted by Mendip District Council (ref TEN/26/0912). Please drink responsibly and look after the field - it is a working farm and we would like to be asked back.'

THE DEADLINE
The printer needs the press file by Wednesday 23 September. They want three working days after that, so the 23rd is hard, not hopeful. If something cannot be done in time, tell us now, not on the 22nd.

AND
Please tell us anything you find that we should know before it goes to print. We would far rather hear it from you than find it framed on a kitchen wall.

Act Name,Stage,Day,Set Time,Biography,@Image
Cole Harrow Band,The Barn Stage,Saturday,6:00pm,"A four-piece out of Bristol trading in swampy, foot-stomping Americana. Slide guitar, a Hammond organ that has seen things, and a rhythm section that does not stop. They played the late slot last year and we asked them straight back.",lanternwood_press_photo_03.jpg
Rue & the Ravens,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,1:00pm,"Dark, gothic folk from the edge of the moor. A cello, a harmonium, close harmonies and songs about the sea taking people. Beautiful and a little haunting, and exactly right for a Sunday afternoon.",lanternwood_press_photo_12.jpg
The Hollow Pines,The Barn Stage,Saturday,9:00pm,"The Hollow Pines have spent the better part of a decade turning small rooms into something close to church. What began as two brothers harmonising over a single guitar at a kitchen table in the Mendips has grown, slowly and stubbornly, into a five-piece that can fill a field without ever raising its voice too far. Their songs are built from the ordinary business of staying somewhere: the drive home in the dark, the field you grew up beside, the people who leave and the people who do not. Three albums in, they have earned a following that treats every show like a reunion, singing the choruses back word for word before the band has finished them. We have wanted them at Lanternwood since the very first year, and we are proud beyond all measure to have them close the Saturday night. Bring a voice. You are going to be using it.",lanternwood_press_photo_04.jpg
Delia Marsh,The Barn Stage,Sunday,2:00pm,"Delia plays the harp and sings like the room has gone quiet even when it has not. Her debut record came out this spring.",lanternwood_press_photo_08.jpg
Fenwick & Doon,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,1:00pm,"A duo, a fiddle and a battered parlour guitar, and two voices that have been finishing each other's lines for twenty years. Traditional tunes, mostly, played the way they were meant to be. You will be dancing whether you meant to or not.",lanternwood_press_photo_05.jpg
The Copper Kettles,The Barn Stage,Sunday,4:00pm,"A skiffle revival band who take it all extremely seriously and not seriously at all, in equal measure. Washboard, tea-chest bass, and a kazoo when the mood takes them. Deeply silly, genuinely brilliant, and a great deal of fun.",lanternwood_press_photo_09.jpg
Odessa Frame,The Barn Stage,Saturday,4:00pm,"Odessa writes quiet songs and sings them louder than you expect. She has toured the folk clubs for six years with just a guitar and a suitcase, and this is her first festival main stage. Come early; she opens gently.",lanternwood_press_photo_02.jpg
Ambrose Fell,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,5:00pm,"Ambrose is a one-man band in the proper sense: kick drum, guitar, harmonica and a stomp box, running the whole thing himself. Ragged, joyful, and much bigger than it has any right to be. A brilliant way to close the Orchard Stage.",lanternwood_press_photo_14.jpg
Marla Vance & the Tallgrass,The Barn Stage,Sunday,8:30pm,"There are voices you hear and voices you feel in your chest, and Marla Vance has spent thirty years proving she has the second kind. She came up singing in touring roadhouse bands long before anyone was writing her name at the top of a poster, and she has never once forgotten what a live room is actually for. The Tallgrass, her band of many years, read her like weather, swelling and dropping back so that the songs breathe around her. Together they make music that manages to sound brand new and like something you have always somehow known, all dust and warmth with a low ache running underneath it. To have her closing our Sunday, out in a field, as the last of the light goes, is the exact thing this committee dreamed about when we started the festival on nothing but nerve and a borrowed marquee. Do not miss a second of it. Stay for the very last note.",lanternwood_press_photo_11.jpg
The Salt Marsh Ramblers,The Barn Stage,Saturday,2:00pm,"Five friends from the Levels who have been playing pub back rooms and barn dances since school. Fiddle, banjo, guitar, double bass and a great deal of shouting. Expect reels, murder ballads and at least one song about flooding.",lanternwood_press_photo_01.jpg
Junction Road Revival,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,5:00pm,"Six of them, three horns, and absolutely no interest in you standing still. Junction Road Revival play gospel soul and old rhythm and blues like the roof is already coming off. If your feet hurt on Sunday morning, this is why.",lanternwood_press_photo_07.jpg
The Threshing Floor,The Orchard Stage,Sunday,3:00pm,"A young band making very old music sound urgent again. Bouzouki, fiddle, bodhran and a frontman whose stories between songs are almost as good as the songs. Ones to watch, and you saw them here.",lanternwood_press_photo_13.jpg
The Bramble Sisters,The Orchard Stage,Saturday,3:00pm,"The Bramble Sisters are not sisters, and only one of them is called Bramble, but the name stuck the way the good ones do. The three of them met singing in a chapel choir and discovered, somewhere between the hymns, that their voices did something strange and lovely when they leaned into a minor chord together. For eight years now they have carried that sound around the country, unaccompanied for whole songs at a time, letting three voices do the work of a full band. Their set moves from old shape-note hymns to their own writing and back again without ever quite telling you where the seam was. It is the kind of thing that can stop a noisy field halfway through a sentence. We have put them on the Orchard Stage in the afternoon light entirely on purpose. Find a bale of hay, sit yourself down, and let them get to work on you.",lanternwood_press_photo_06.jpg
Waylon Pike Trio,The Barn Stage,Sunday,6:00pm,"Waylon Pike has been playing guitar longer than most of the committee has been alive, and it shows in every unhurried note. With brush drums and an upright bass behind him, the trio plays a warm, late-afternoon kind of blues. Perfect for the graveyard slot between lunch and the headliner.",lanternwood_press_photo_10.jpg

CELLAR & CRU - autumn selection, how I'd talk you through it (Rob)

THE SHAPE OF THE BAY
Fourteen wines. Two of them anchor the bay and everything else sits around them: the Cote Brune Syrah from Domaine des Escaliers, 2019, and the Cascina Voltone Nebbiolo, 2016. Those are the two people photograph the card of and come back for at Christmas. They earn the top of the bay.

THE TWO I WANT PEOPLE TO TRY
The two I will put a card in someone's hand for are the Cave de Trevigne co-op red at fourteen pounds - it drinks miles above its price if you open it an hour before - and the Domaine Ravel Morgon, the one that changes how people think about Beaujolais. If a card sells one bottle of each this month I'm happy.

THE WHITES AND THE ROSE
The Muscadet is the everyday white, sur lie, saline, fourteen pounds, buy it by the case. Alsace Riesling, Chablis, the Mosel Kabinett and the Gruner are the four that do the work on the white shelf. The Sancerre is on the list but I have not got a picture of it - we ran out of evening, so flag it. The Provence rose and the Vermentino round it off.

ON THE SCORES
We print the score where there is one and we leave the space empty where there is not. I do not chase them and I will not inflate them. A score is one reader's note, printed small, under the wine, never over it. The co-op red has no score and I do not want one invented for it.

ON THE NOTES
The long notes on the two anchors and the two I'm pushing are mine, written the way I would say them at the counter. The shorter ones came off the buyer's card. Do not shorten mine to make them fit the card - if they will not fit, tell me and I will cut them myself before it prints.

CONTINENTAL CUP 2026 — CARD PRINTER SPEC (what we and the licensing partner need back)

TRIM & STOCK
- Card trim: 63.5 x 88.9 mm portrait (2.5 x 3.5 in), the same as last season's team-set file.
- BLEED: we require 3 mm bleed on all four sides on the press-ready file. Note: last season's PDF was supplied with no bleed box; if you build off it, tell us plainly what can and cannot be done about bleed.
- Print resolution: 600 dpi at trim. A full card at trim is therefore 1500 x 2100 px.

FRAMES (as we hold the geometry; confirm against the converted document)
- PHOTO frame: 52.0 x 74.0 mm, i.e. about 1230 x 1748 px at 600 dpi. Placed photography must reach this at native scale. Do NOT upscale to fill it — a soft interpolated card is a reject.
- MARK frame: 9.5 x 9.5 mm, top-left, i.e. about 224 x 224 px at 600 dpi. The mark prints reversed on the dark field. It has to still read as our mark at that size.
- Text: player name, squad number, position, club line, set year are five separate fields.

ORDER
- The press file runs the WHOLE STOCKED SQUAD, one player per page, in SQUAD-NUMBER ORDER (1, 2, 3 ... ascending). The roster export is not in that order. Do not ship it in the order it arrived.

PROOFS
- Proofs for licensing sign-off must be rendered at 600 dpi at trim (1500 x 2100 px), embedded density set. A screen-scale page raster is not a proof.

PER-PLAYER FILES (the partner distributes these individually)
- One single-card PDF per stocked player, named: CUP26_<squadnumber-2digit>_<Surname>.pdf (e.g. CUP26_07_Ferraz.pdf, CUP26_09_Okoye.pdf). The name on the file MUST be the player on the card inside it — the partner keys distribution off the filename, so a mislabelled file ships to the wrong channel.

DELIVERY
- One ordered multi-page press file, eighteen named single-card files, the proofs, and a note of anything about this spec the supplied file cannot meet.

HALDEN GREENS — HOOK LINES + CATEGORY COMPLIANCE (from the growth lead)

SIX HOOKS. We think three of them are the strong ones. You tell us which three, and tell us plainly which ones you would not run and why.

H1  I kept drinking it. That's the whole review.
H2  Greens I don't have to talk myself into.
H3  It's greens. You drink them in the morning. That's it.
H4  Absorbs better than the multivitamin you gave up on.
H5  Clears the bloating other greens powders leave you with.
H6  I started drinking this every morning before work and I honestly just kept going.

-----------------------------------------------------------------
CATEGORY COMPLIANCE SHEET (one page, from our regulatory file)
Anything on this list does NOT run, however good the line reads. This sheet does not flag individual hooks; that judgement is yours.

1. NO COMPARATIVE SUPERIORITY. We may not claim the product works better, absorbs better, or is more effective than any other product, category, brand or competitor. "better than", "more absorbable than", "beats", "outperforms" — all out.
2. NO DISEASE / CONDITION CLAIMS. We may not say the product treats, cures, clears, fixes, prevents or relieves any condition or symptom — this explicitly includes bloating, fatigue, inflammation and deficiency.
3. NO "clinically proven" or "doctor recommended" — we hold no substantiation on file.
4. NO absolute health outcomes: no "boosts immunity", "detoxes", "balances hormones".
5. NO before/after or guaranteed-result language.

PERMITTED: subjective, first-person, habit-and-taste language. Structure/function only, hedged, and never by comparison. "I kept drinking it", "don't have to talk myself into it", "in the morning" are all fine.

A NOTE ON LENGTH (not a compliance matter): a hook has to land in the first read at vertical caption size. If a line has to be shrunk to fit, it has stopped being a hook.

STERLING ROW - notes for whoever produces the channel package

WHO WE ARE
Nine full-floor residences in a converted warehouse block. They start just over four million dollars. We sell them one at a time, to buyers who are not in a hurry and who have seen everything. The channel is where most of them meet me first, so every video has to feel made by one hand.

THE RESTRAINT (this is the whole proposition)
Quiet, near-neutral, almost no text on screen. The grade sits near neutral and slightly cool: clean whites, no crushed blacks, no warm saturated push. Motion is slow and largely static. On-screen text is minimal and small. The wordmark reproduces modestly. Anything that looks like a promotion - fast cuts, a saturated warm grade, large benefit captions, a price burned across the frame - reads at this tier as a building that is struggling to sell, and that ends a four-million-dollar conversation. Do not go the other way into pure atmosphere either: a qualified buyer still needs the floor, the square footage and the exposure before she asks to view.

APPROVED LANGUAGE
Tagline: "Nine residences. No hurry."
Voice, spare and composed: "Nine residences. Full floor. Sold one at a time, to buyers in no hurry."
Say: full-floor residence, converted warehouse, exposure, ceiling height, outdoor space.
Never say: luxury lifestyle, act now, limited time, dream home, or anything that sounds like it is selling.

TYPE
One reassuring, near-neutral pairing. No high-contrast display serif (reads as a perfume advert at this tier). No heavy grotesque (reads as a development marketing brochure). Text sits small and calm. Name the family, foundry and the actual weight you use, per role, in the handover.

THE CHANNEL COVER
Every cover still is cut to 2560 x 1440 px. It cannot be a person standing next to a window with a graphic pointing at it. It has to earn a click on composition alone, and it must not embarrass a buyer who forwards it to her advisor.

THE WORDMARK
The only surviving version is the handheld photograph of the cast-brass plaque in the lobby. There is no vector file and no clean scan. Whatever you deliver has to still read as that wordmark, recovered from the plaque rather than redrawn into a font, and it has to read as the words at the small size it actually sits at on the end card - not just at canvas size.

MERIDIAN ACADEMY - Operations Analytics for Working Managers
Lesson 4: Reconciling the Numbers (approved outline, written before recording)

This is the plan we shot from. Roughly forty minutes. Plain and unhurried, talking to a peer.

Beat 1 - Where the gap comes from
Objective: the learner can explain why the ledger and the operational feed never agree on the first pass, and name the three causes - timing, mapping and manual edits.

Beat 2 - Lining up the two sources
Objective: the learner can set the ledger balance and the ops-feed balance side by side for the same period and say which figure each system is authoritative for.

Beat 3 - Building the reconciliation model (the roll-forward)
Objective: the learner can build a roll-forward that bridges last month's agreed closing balance to this month's, posting each movement once in date order so the ending figure traces back line by line. THIS IS THE HEART OF THE LESSON.

Beat 4 - Setting a materiality threshold
Objective: the learner can choose the dollar line below which a reconciling difference is logged but not chased, so the hours spent investigating never cost more than the variance itself.

Beat 5 - Working one real exception end to end
Objective: the learner can trace a single variance to its cause using a real worked example (the recorded customer call), and decide what carries forward and what does not.

Beat 6 - Handing it to your manager
Objective: the learner can present the reconciliation as a one-page bridge, every line explained, rather than a raw spreadsheet.

Keep it plain. No slides-with-arrows, no hype. This is the lesson people stop on, so slow down and make the walkthrough land.

Lane changes,"1. Check your interior mirror for what is behind you. 2. Check the door mirror on the side you are moving to. 3. Signal in good time. 4. Take a quick glance over your shoulder to clear the blind spot. 5. Move across smoothly in one steady movement. 6. Cancel the signal and settle into the new lane.","One lane at a time. Never two at once.",milepost_road_still_06.jpg
Right turns,"1. Slow down early and get into the correct position. 2. Signal right in good time. 3. Check your mirrors and the road you are turning into. 4. Take the turn at a speed that lets you stay in your own lane. 5. Straighten up and build speed gently once you are round.","Slow in, steady out.",milepost_road_still_03.jpg
Left turns across traffic,"1. Begin slowing well before the junction. 2. Move to the correct position near the centre line. 3. Signal left across the oncoming lane in good time. 4. Stop at the give-way line if you cannot see a clear gap. 5. Watch the oncoming traffic and judge the gaps, not the cars. 6. Look through the turn to where you want to end up. 7. Check for pedestrians crossing the road you are entering. 8. Wait for a gap you are certain of, not one you are hoping for. 9. When the gap is clear, turn smoothly across the lane. 10. Keep your wheels straight while you wait so a knock will not push you forward. 11. Complete the turn into your own lane and cancel the signal.","When in doubt, wait. A missed gap costs seconds; a wrong one costs more.",milepost_road_still_02.jpg
Roundabouts,"1. Read the signs and road markings on the approach. 2. Slow down early and choose your lane before you arrive. 3. Give way to traffic already on the roundabout, usually from your left. 4. Wait for a gap and enter without stopping if you can. 5. Keep to your lane and follow the markings round. 6. Signal left as you pass the exit before the one you want. 7. Leave the roundabout in your lane and check your mirror.","Look left, take your time, and keep moving when it is clear.",milepost_roundabout_ref.jpg
Parallel parking,"1. Find a space at least a car and a half long. 2. Pull up level with the car in front, about half a metre out. 3. Check your mirrors and blind spot for anything coming. 4. Select reverse and begin backing slowly. 5. When your back wheels are level with the other car's bumper, turn the wheel toward the kerb. 6. Bring the car back at a shallow angle. 7. When the front clears the parked car, straighten the wheel. 8. Reverse gently until you are parallel with the kerb. 9. Adjust forward and back until you are centred in the space.","Slow and small. Let the wheel do the work.",milepost_road_still_05.jpg
Merging,"1. Build your speed along the slip road to match the traffic. 2. Check your mirrors as you go. 3. Look for a gap in the lane you are joining. 4. Signal to show where you are going. 5. Keep glancing between the road ahead and your mirror. 6. Ease into the gap at matching speed. 7. Do not stop on the slip road unless you have to. 8. Cancel your signal and keep a safe distance.","Match the speed, find the gap, ease in.",milepost_road_still_04.jpg
Four-way stops,"1. Come to a full stop at the line, every time. 2. The first vehicle to stop is the first to go. 3. If two of you arrive together, the one on the right goes first. 4. When it is your turn, move off clearly so others know.","Full stop, then first come, first go.",milepost_road_still_01.jpg
Hazard recognition,"1. Keep scanning far ahead, not just the car in front. 2. Ask what could happen next and cover the brake. 3. Slow down before a hazard, not on top of it.","See it early, and you have time.",milepost_road_still_06.jpg
